title: The Talmud Page: These and These
hook: Hasidic, Lithuanian, Sephardi, modern and women's voices, all in one conversation
carry: the talmud keeps both sides: these and these
tomorrow: Moses sat in a class and couldn't follow it. why was he comforted?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Baba Sali: the priests say the words, and God does the blessing. Blessings of the humble. Today, all the voices of this stretch, on one page.
screen: `BLESSINGS OF THE HUMBLE.` → `ALL THE VOICES, ONE PAGE.`

segments.voice: A kitchen table, cleared after dinner. An old man unfolds one large printed page and smooths it flat with both hands. His granddaughter leans in, expecting a paragraph. Instead there's a block of text in the middle, and around it, in smaller type, more text, and around that, more again, like a group chat where everyone is replying to everyone, except some of them lived centuries apart. She asks the obvious thing: who's talking? He taps the middle, then the edges. Everyone, he says. That's the point.
screen: `ONE BIG PAGE ON THE TABLE.` → `TEXT AROUND TEXT AROUND TEXT.` → `WHO'S TALKING? EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: That's a page of Talmud, and it's built like a conversation. In the center sits the Mishnah, and the Gemara, the sages' long discussion of it. On the inside margin, Rashi, the great commentator, explaining word by word. On the outside, the Tosafot, a circle of later scholars arguing with Rashi and with each other. Then more notes, from more generations, pressed in at the edges. Nobody cleared the table before the next voice sat down. And here is the detail to tell a friend: the losing opinions stay on the page. The Mishnah itself asks why it records a minority view if the law follows the majority, and answers, so that a later court could lean on it someday. The Talmud tells of a heavenly voice settling a long dispute between two schools: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the house of Hillel. Both sides kept. Now look back at the voices of these weeks and see them on that page. Rebbe Nachman finding the good point. Rabbi Soloveitchik, from a Lithuanian line of learning, bringing holiness into the details. Nechama Leibowitz asking for the real question. Rabbi Ovadia Yosef restoring Sephardi custom. Heschel's wonder, Buber's you. Henrietta Szold saying Kaddish herself, and a woman's tkhine in three languages. They didn't always agree, and some would have argued hard across the table. That's not a flaw in the tradition. It is the tradition. One long conversation, still going, with a seat left open at the edge.
screen: `MISHNAH AND GEMARA IN THE CENTER.` · `RASHI INSIDE, TOSAFOT OUTSIDE.` · `THE LOSING VIEWS STAY.` · `THESE AND THESE.` · then, large: `ONE LONG CONVERSATION.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the voices from these weeks that stayed with you: a philosopher, a poet, a rabbi, a woman who said Kaddish herself. Let each one get a finger and a moment of thanks. Then settle on one, your favorite so far, and hold that name for the rest of the sit.
screen: `ONE FINGER PER VOICE.` · `A MOMENT OF THANKS EACH.` · `HOLD YOUR FAVORITE.`

segments.voice: One long conversation: the Talmud page, with every generation's voice around the center, the losing views kept.
Your line: the Talmud keeps both sides, these and these. Every voice kept, even the ones who lost. That's day one thousand six hundred forty-six.

screen: `DAY 1646 COUNTS.` → `LATER VOICES · 39 OF 40.` → `TOMORROW: MOSES COULDN'T FOLLOW THE CLASS. WHY COMFORTED?`

fork.setup: your family's group chat splits over where to hold the reunion, and your uncle wants to delete the losing side's messages to 'keep it clean.' what does the Talmud page suggest?
options: keep them: a losing view can matter later, and everyone stays at the table.
delete them: once a decision's made, the old arguments only cause trouble.
start a new chat with only the side that won, so it feels settled.
fork.reveal: the Mishnah keeps minority views so a later court can lean on them, and the Talmud calls both schools the words of the living God. both sides kept.

chat.says: saba gave me a printed Talmud page for the trip. it's literally people arguing?? why is that a gift
options: Because the arguing is the gift: every voice kept, even the losers, and room for yours.
It isn't arguing; the margins are footnotes that just agree with the middle part.
Because only the middle counts. The margins are extra you can skip for now.
chat.meaning: A Talmud page keeps generations of voices around the center, losing views included. Giving it is inviting her into the conversation.

tie.story: When the schools of Hillel and Shammai argued, the Talmud says a heavenly voice called both the words of the living God, and both stayed on the page.
tie.friend: Saba's Talmud page invites Noa into that argument, with a seat at the edge for her.
tie.you: whose voice would you add to the page?

Mishnah.meaning: the first written collection of rabbinic law

Gemara.meaning: the sages' discussion of the Mishnah

Rashi.meaning: a medieval commentator who explains the Talmud word by word

Tosafot.meaning: later scholars whose notes fill the Talmud's outer margin

Hillel.meaning: a sage whose school's rulings the law usually follows
